title: 1 Chronicles 28:11–21
context: David gives Solomon the plans for the temple, its rooms, courts, and treasuries, the divisions of priests and Levites, and the weights of gold and silver for the vessels, lampstands, tables, altar of incense, and the cherubim over the ark. He says he was made to understand all this in writing from the LORD’s hand, and he encourages Solomon to be strong and courageous, for the LORD will not fail him. Both traditions read this as shared ground; the text does not describe the form of the writing, and the parallel with the pattern shown to Moses (Exod 25:9, 40) is noted as a reading.

verses.text: Then David gave to Solomon his son the plans for the porch of the temple, for its houses, for its treasuries, for its upper rooms, for its inner rooms, for the place of the mercy seat;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then David gave to Solomon his son the plans for the porch of the temple, for its houses, for its treasuries, for its upper rooms, for its inner rooms, for the place of the mercy seat.” Arminian readers note the careful handing on of the work.

The mercy seat recalls the ark’s cover in the tabernacle (Exod 25:17–22).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see continuity between tabernacle and temple, both ordered by God.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: worship is to be offered as God directs, and the mercy seat is the place associated with atonement and God’s presence.

verses.text: and the plans of all that he had by the Spirit, for the courts of the LORD’s house, for all the surrounding rooms, for the treasuries of God’s house, and for the treasuries of the dedicated things;
verses.arminianNotes:
David gives “the plans of all that he had by the Spirit, for the courts of the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note that WEB reads “the Spirit”; translations differ on whether the phrase refers to God’s Spirit or to what David had in his own spirit or mind.

The wording is left open here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the difference among translations and do not press it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: 28:19 states that the plans came from the LORD, whatever the precise sense of this phrase.

verses.text: also for the divisions of the priests and the Levites, for all the work of the service of the LORD’s house, and for all the vessels of service in the LORD’s house—
verses.arminianNotes:
The plans include “the divisions of the priests and the Levites, for all the work of the service of the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note that the plans cover people and service as well as buildings.

The divisions are set out in 1 Chronicles 23–26.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the ordering of worship as part of God’s provision for his house.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: faithful worship involves ordered service, not only a building.

verses.text: of gold by weight for the gold for all vessels of every kind of service, for all the vessels of silver by weight, for all vessels of every kind of service;
verses.arminianNotes:
The gold and silver are given “by weight” for the vessels of every kind of service. Arminian readers note the precision with which the materials are assigned.

The detail shows care for what will be offered to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same care as fitting reverence for the LORD’s house.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the weights are part of a record of faithful preparation, and the verse need not be pressed beyond that.

verses.text: by weight also for the lamp stands of gold, and for its lamps, of gold, by weight for every lamp stand and for its lamps; and for the lamp stands of silver, by weight for every lamp stand and for its lamps, according to the use of every lamp stand;
verses.arminianNotes:
The weights are given for the lampstands of gold and silver and their lamps, “according to the use of every lamp stand.” Arminian readers note that each item has its purpose.

The lampstands recall the tabernacle lampstand (Exod 25:31–40).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see continuity with the tabernacle furnishings.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the temple continues the worship God established through Moses.

verses.text: and the gold by weight for the tables of show bread, for every table; and silver for the tables of silver;
verses.arminianNotes:
Gold is given “for the tables of show bread, for every table; and silver for the tables of silver.” Arminian readers note the provision for the bread set before the LORD.

The tabernacle had one table (Exod 25:23–30); the temple plans speak of tables.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the bread of the presence continued in the temple.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the furnishings express God’s fellowship with his people.

verses.text: and the forks, the basins, and the cups, of pure gold; and for the golden bowls by weight for every bowl; and for the silver bowls by weight for every bowl;
verses.arminianNotes:
The forks, basins, and cups are to be “of pure gold,” and the bowls of gold and silver are weighed. Arminian readers note the attention given to even small vessels.

Nothing in God’s service is too small to matter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same reverence extended to every detail of the service.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: ordinary items, used in worship, are treated as holy.

verses.text: and for the altar of incense, refined gold by weight; and gold for the plans for the chariot, and the cherubim that spread out and cover the ark of the LORD’s covenant.
verses.arminianNotes:
Refined gold is given for the altar of incense, and gold “for the plans for the chariot, and the cherubim that spread out and cover the ark.” Arminian readers note the image of the cherubim as a chariot, which some connect with passages such as Psalm 18:10.

The meaning of “chariot” here is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the cherubim over the ark as signs of God’s throne and presence.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and do not press the image further than the text goes.

verses.text: “All this”, David said, “I have been made to understand in writing from the LORD’s hand, even all the works of this pattern.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “I have been made to understand in writing from the LORD’s hand, even all the works of this pattern.” Arminian readers note that the plans are presented as given by God, not invented by David.

The text does not describe the form of the writing or how it was given.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a parallel with the pattern shown to Moses (Exod 25:9, 40), which is a reading many hold.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the temple is to be built as the LORD directed, and neither tradition needs to reconstruct the plans beyond what the text says.

verses.text: David said to Solomon his son, “Be strong and courageous, and do it. Don’t be afraid, nor be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you, until all the work for the service of the LORD’s house is finished.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Be strong and courageous, and do it. Don’t be afraid, nor be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.” Arminian readers note the encouragement that echoes Deuteronomy 31:6–8 and Joshua 1:5–9.

God’s presence makes the task possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness as the ground of Solomon’s courage (cf. Heb 13:5).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the promise of God’s presence is given “until all the work for the service of the LORD’s house is finished.”

verses.text: Behold, there are the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of God’s house. Every willing man who has skill for any kind of service shall be with you in all kinds of work. Also the captains and all the people will be entirely at your command.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David points to the priests and Levites and says, “Every willing man who has skill for any kind of service shall be with you.” Arminian readers note the willing participation of the people.

The phrase recalls the willing workers of the tabernacle (Exod 35:10; 36:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God providing the people and skills needed for his work.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: willing service and God’s provision go together.
